steps: Shape your dominant hand into a G, pinching your thumb and index finger into a small pincer.
Extend the index finger of your non-dominant hand and hold it up in front of your chest.
Tap the side of your dominant G hand once against the side of your non-dominant index finger.
Angle your dominant palm toward the non-dominant hand and the non-dominant palm back toward it.
Use a single tap for the verb print; tap twice to sign the noun newspaper.
tip: “Printing” is signed with the base PRINT sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a G, pinching your thumb and index finger into a small pincer.
Extend the index finger of your non-dominant hand and hold it up in front of your chest.
Tap the side of your dominant G hand once against the side of your non-dominant index finger.
Angle your dominant palm toward the non-dominant hand and the non-dominant palm back toward it.
Use a single tap for the verb print; tap twice to sign the noun newspaper.
tip: Past form of “Print” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a slightly curved cup, letting your fingers relax and curve gently.
Hold the curved hand up in front of your chest in neutral signing space.
Twist the hand once at the wrist, rotating it through a single smooth turn.
Let your palm orientation roll with the twist instead of holding it fixed.
Purse your lips and narrow your eyes slightly, as if studying two things side by side.
tip: “Compares” is signed with the base COMPARE sign.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a slightly curved cup, letting your fingers relax and curve gently.

Purse your lips and narrow your eyes slightly, as if studying two things side by side.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a slightly curved cup, letting your fingers relax and curve gently.

Purse your lips and narrow your eyes slightly, as if studying two things side by side.

steps: Hold both hands flat with the fingers together, palms facing each other at chest height.
Move your flat hands apart to show the two opposite walls of the room.
Bend both hands at the knuckles so they form right angles like bent frames.
Bring the bent hands back toward each other to trace the front and back walls.
Keep your palms angled inward so the hands sketch a small square room floating in the air.
Hold a neutral expression — context decides whether this shape means ROOM or BOX.
tip: Plural of “Room” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both flat hands up with the palms facing each other at chest height.
Separate the flat hands sideways to show the two walls of the box.
Bend both hands at the knuckles into right-angle shapes.
Move the bent hands toward each other to mark the front and back of the box.
Angle your palms inward so the hands outline a small box floating in front of you.
Keep a plain expression — the identical sign means ROOM when the topic is a room.
tip: Plural of “Box” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant index finger upright in front of your chest.
Make a fist with your dominant hand, the thumb resting along the side like an A handshape.
Press the thumb side of the fist against the top edge of the upright index finger.
Brush the fist back and forth along the finger two or three times, as if polishing a shoe.
Keep both palms facing sideways while the brushing stays short and quick.
Stay relaxed and neutral — swap the A fist for a T fist only if you must mark the English word.
tip: Plural of “Training” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into open F handshapes, thumb and index forming loose circles.
Hold the two F hands apart in front of your chest with the palms facing each other.
Bring the hands together so the two F circles interlock like links of a chain.
Tug the linked hands gently outward once to show the connection holds firm.
Keep your fingers relaxed so the link reads as two small rings hooking together.
Wear a purposeful, neutral expression — this is the 'connect two things together' version of JOIN.
tip: “Joins” is signed with the base JOIN sign.

steps: Shape both hands into open F handshapes, thumb and index forming loose circles.
Hold the two F hands apart in front of your chest with the palms facing each other.
Bring the hands together so the two F circles interlock like links of a chain.
Tug the linked hands gently outward once to show the connection holds firm.
Keep your fingers relaxed so the link reads as two small rings hooking together.
Wear a purposeful, neutral expression — this is the 'connect two things together' version of JOIN.
tip: “Joining” is signed with the base JOIN sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Shape both hands into open F handshapes, thumb and index forming loose circles.
Hold the two F hands apart in front of your chest with the palms facing each other.
Bring the hands together so the two F circles interlock like links of a chain.
Tug the linked hands gently outward once to show the connection holds firm.
Keep your fingers relaxed so the link reads as two small rings hooking together.
Wear a purposeful, neutral expression — this is the 'connect two things together' version of JOIN.
tip: Past form of “Join” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Pinch your dominant index finger against your thumb tip, like gripping a small token.
Hold the pinched fingers out in front of your chest with the palm facing down.
Close the pinch on an imaginary option and lift the hand upward toward yourself.
Draw the hand back to your body in one smooth, decisive sweep.
Keep the wrist steady and the palm facing down through the whole pull-in motion.
Nod once as you finish — selecting is a firm and deliberate choice.
tip: “Selects” is signed with the base SELECT sign.

steps: Pinch your dominant index finger against your thumb tip, like gripping a small token.
Hold the pinched fingers out in front of your chest with the palm facing down.
Close the pinch on an imaginary option and lift the hand upward toward yourself.
Draw the hand back to your body in one smooth, decisive sweep.
Keep the wrist steady and the palm facing down through the whole pull-in motion.
Nod once as you finish — selecting is a firm and deliberate choice.

steps: Pinch your dominant index finger against your thumb tip, like gripping a small token.
Hold the pinched fingers out in front of your chest with the palm facing down.

steps: Shape both hands into T handshapes, each index finger laid across the top of its thumb.
Touch the fingertips of both T hands together in front of your chest.
Circle both hands outward together, tracing a wide loop like teammates around a table.
Bring the hands back around so the fingertips meet again at the center.
Keep the two hands mirroring each other through the entire circle.
Stay warm and neutral — the circle reads as a group, and the T hands say team.
tip: Plural of “Team” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed curved-5 shapes, fingers loosely curled like soft claws.
Hold the hands up at chest height with the palms facing slightly forward.
Push both hands forward together in one smooth motion.
As the hands travel, twist both wrists so the palms turn slightly backward.
Imagine sliding your hands around the sides of a large invisible ball.
Keep your expression neutral — this GROUP sign doubles as CATEGORY, CLASS, or COLLECTION.
tip: Plural of “Category” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a W, three fingers up and the thumb holding the pinky.
Hold the W in front of your chest at a comfortable height, palm angled slightly forward.
Sweep the whole hand sideways to your left in one short, level motion.
Keep the W handshape frozen and the palm steady through the sweep.
Picture a map: west sits at the left edge, so the W travels toward it.
Keep your face neutral and the movement crisp — direction signs stay small and clear.
tip: Plural of “West” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an A handshape with both hands: a fist with the thumb resting along the side.
Stack the hands at your chest with your dominant fist resting on your non-dominant fist.
Thrust both hands straight up once with one large, quick upward movement.
End with the hands floating an inch or two off your chest, palms still facing in.
Keep a neutral expression — the double-tap version of this sign means ADDRESS instead.
tip: Past form of “Live” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and horizontal in front of you as the tabletop.
Make a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers together, palm facing down.
Lay the dominant hand on top of the non-dominant hand to show the flat top surface.
Pat the base hand twice with short downward taps of the dominant hand.
Keep the base hand steady while the taps sketch out the flat tabletop.
tip: Plural of “Table” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand upright with the fingers together, like a screen edge.
Spread all five fingers of your dominant hand into a 5 handshape.
Press the dominant hand against the edge of the upright hand so it can pivot.
Twist your dominant wrist side to side while it stays pressed to the base hand.
Keep the twisting small and quick, as if film frames were flickering past.
Stay neutral-faced — the same sign is used for a video as well as a movie.
tip: Plural of “Movie” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend your non-dominant hand in front of you in a flat handshape, palm up.
Make an X handshape with your dominant hand — a fist with a bent index finger — palm facing back.
Bring the bent index finger down to strike the palm of the base hand.
Use one sharp downward tap of the X finger against the palm.
Keep a neutral expression — this sign also covers fee, fine, and sometimes tax.
tip: Plural of “Cost” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up in front of your chest.
Extend your dominant index finger straight up in a 1 handshape.
Rest the fingertip on the heel of the base hand's palm so your wrist can pivot.
Give one very quick small tick with the fingertip, moving only from the wrist.
Keep the tick tiny and fast — the same sign done slower and larger means MINUTE.
tip: Plural of “Second” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Raise both hands to the sides of your head with your fingers loosely curved and spread.
Angle your palms inward toward each other, holding the hands about shoulder-width apart.
Keep your elbows relaxed and low so the hands frame the space beside your temples.
Trace small circles in the air with both hands at the same time.
Keep the motion tight and close to your head, as if outlining the subject you are naming.
Wear a plain, neutral expression — the same sign doubles as QUOTE, SUBJECT, and TITLE.
tip: Plural of “Topic” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into loose fists with the thumbs resting up on top.
Hold the fists at chest height, about a shoulder-width apart in neutral space.
Turn your palms to face each other so the two fists mirror one another.
Push both hands straight forward together in one smooth, level motion.
Keep the fist shapes frozen while they travel, as if paving a stretch of road.
Stay neutral-faced — the same production signs WAY, PATH, and ROAD.
tip: Plural of “Street” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend your non-dominant hand in front of you, palm facing up with the fingers together.
Form your dominant hand into an X: a fist with the index finger bent at the knuckle.
Hold the X hand above the open palm with its own palm facing back toward you.
Tap the bent index finger down onto the palm once with a short, sharp motion.
Keep your face neutral and the base hand perfectly still during the tap.
tip: Plural of “Tax” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into L handshapes, thumb and index finger opened at a right angle.
Bring the hands together so the index fingertips touch in front of your chest.
Pull the L hands apart sideways in one smooth motion.
Add a slight twisting shake of the forearms as the hands separate.
tip: Plural of “Language” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an open hand with the fingers together and slightly relaxed.
Place the palm of the hand against the side of your cheek, near the chin.
Stroke downward along your cheek as if pulling at an imaginary beard.
Exaggerate the length of the stroke, because a longer pull means more experience.
Keep your face relaxed and thoughtful, like an elder recalling a long life.
tip: Plural of “Experience” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand up in front of you with the thumb and index finger pinched together.
Imagine you are holding a small metal key between the pinched fingertips.
Push the imaginary key forward into an imaginary lock at chest height.
Twist your wrist twice, as if turning the key inside the lock.
Keep the palm facing sideways while twisting; a single twist instead means the verb to lock.
tip: Plural of “Key” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands open with the fingers together and the palms facing inward.
Touch your fingertips to the upper part of your torso, near the chest.
Move both hands downward together and touch the lower part of your torso.
Make the two touches distinct, first high and then low, to outline the whole body.
Keep your expression neutral; the sign simply marks the full span of the torso.
tip: Plural of “Body” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an E handshape, with the fingers curled and the thumb tucked.
Hold the E hand up at shoulder height with the palm facing forward.
Move the hand in a short straight line toward your right.
Keep the handshape fixed while it travels; east sits to the right on a map.
Use a neutral face, and note the same E hand moves other ways for north, south, and west.
tip: Plural of “East” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: To introduce the word in a new conversation, fingerspell P-A-S-S-W-O-R-D with your dominant hand.
Shape the same hand into an A handshape, a fist with the thumb pressed along the side.
Tap your lips twice with the back of the thumb, keeping the palm facing toward you.
Keep the taps light and quick; once the meaning is clear, the sign alone can mean password.
Mouth a word shape close to password while signing to mark the intended meaning.
tip: Plural of “Password” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into bent hands, curling all four fingers like claws while the thumbs stay relaxed.
Stack one bent hand on top of the other in front of your chest, as if laying a brick.
Lift the lower hand and stack it on top of the upper one, climbing upward step by step.
Keep climbing with alternating hands for three or four layers to show the rising structure.
Use all four fingers on each hand; this full-handed version marks the noun, a finished building.
tip: Plural of “Building” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a flat B hand with the fingers together and extended.
Hold the B hand steady in front of your chest with the palm facing sideways.
Cross the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand into an R handshape.
Slide the R hand forward along the top edge of the stationary B hand.
Let the R hand drop off the end of the B hand and fall downward to finish.
tip: Plural of “Result” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Point your dominant index finger straight out as the asking handshape.
Hold the pointing hand at chest height, aimed squarely at the person.
Move the hand toward them while the index finger curls into an X hook.
Keep your palm angled toward the person throughout the pulling motion.
Raise your eyebrows with a polite, expectant expression while signing.
tip: “Requests” is signed with the base REQUEST sign.

steps: Point your dominant index finger straight out as the asking handshape.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, fingers curved opposite the thumb like a frame.
Lift the C hand to the side of your eye and hold your other palm up flat.
Bring the C hand down onto the flat palm, as if printing the image onto paper.
Keep the base palm upright and steady while the C hand lands against it.
Hold a neutral expression — context decides whether you mean picture or photograph.
tip: Plural of “Picture” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open your dominant hand into a flat 5, fingers spread with the thumb out.
Hold the open hand just off your cheek, near the temple, without touching it.
Sweep the hand forward in one smooth outward arc toward the future ahead.
Keep the palm facing inward toward your face as the hand travels forward.
Stay neutral in the face; a repeated double arc stretches the meaning to someday.
tip: Plural of “Future” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Raise both hands with all fingers and thumbs extended and slightly spread.
Hold both hands up at chest height in front of your torso.
Bring the two hands together until the fingertips and thumbs meet in the middle.
Keep the palms facing each other as the hands come together.
Do not shrink this to two index fingers — that smaller sign is MEET, not MEETING.
tip: Plural of “Meeting” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape both hands into flat hands, fingers together and perfectly straight.
Press the fingertips of both hands together in front of your chest.
Twist both wrists so the palm orientations trade places in one clean turn.
Start with the dominant palm facing in and the other facing out, then swap them.
Keep your expression neutral — the wrist flip alone carries the sense of change.
tip: “Becomes” is signed with the base BECOME sign.

tip: Past form of “Become” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Shape both hands into K handshapes, with the middle finger resting on the thumb and the index and pinky fingers extended.
Hold your non-dominant K hand out to the side of your body, steady and still as the base.
Swing your dominant K hand in one quick downward motion onto the non-dominant K hand.
Let the pinky-side edge of the dominant hand land firmly on the top of the base hand.
Keep the base hand frozen through the whole movement; only the dominant hand travels.
Pair the sign with a firm, decisive expression when signing it as a command like keep it.
tip: “Keeps” is signed with the base KEEP sign.

steps: Shape both hands into K handshapes, with the middle finger resting on the thumb and the index and pinky fingers extended.
Hold your non-dominant K hand out to the side of your body, steady and still as the base.
Swing your dominant K hand in one quick downward motion onto the non-dominant K hand.
Let the pinky-side edge of the dominant hand land firmly on the top of the base hand.
Keep the base hand frozen through the whole movement; only the dominant hand travels.
Pair the sign with a firm, decisive expression when signing it as a command like keep it.
tip: “Keeping” is signed with the base KEEP sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your non-dominant flat hand out in front of your chest with the palm facing down.
Start your dominant flat hand above and slightly behind the base hand, palm also facing down.
Swoop the dominant hand downward and slide it underneath the base hand from the thumb side.
Arc the hand upward and out through the pinky side, like a small animal slipping into a burrow.
Keep the base hand still and slightly curved so the tunnel underneath it stays clear.
Move with a smooth, single path; repeat the swoop a second, smaller time to mean inside.
tip: “Enters” is signed with the base ENTER sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand up with the index finger pointing upward and the other fingers folded.
Turn the index finger so its side faces your dominant hand.
Brush the pinky-side edge of your dominant flat hand along the side of that index finger.
Slide from the fingertips down toward the thumb in one smooth sweep.
Reverse and sweep back from the thumb toward the fingertips to finish the sharing motion.
Keep the non-dominant hand steady; the back-and-forth pass shows the give-and-take of sharing.
tip: “Sharing” is signed with the base SHARE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand up with the index finger pointing upward and the other fingers folded.
Turn the index finger so its side faces your dominant hand.
Brush the pinky-side edge of your dominant flat hand along the side of that index finger.
Slide from the fingertips down toward the thumb in one smooth sweep.
Reverse and sweep back from the thumb toward the fingertips to finish the sharing motion.
Keep the non-dominant hand steady; the back-and-forth pass shows the give-and-take of sharing.
tip: Past form of “Share” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Shape your dominant hand like a flattened O, pressing your thumb pad up under your fingers.
Keep the fingers straight and pinched together, as if gripping a thin piece of cardboard.
Hold the hand out in front of your waist with the thumb side facing slightly upward.
Move the hand forward and down in one smooth motion, as if setting the object in place.
Stop cleanly at the end of the path to show the item has landed where it belongs.
Tilt the sign toward the person or spot receiving the item to show direction.
tip: “Puts” is signed with the base PUT sign.

steps: Open your dominant hand flat with the fingers together and extended.
Turn the palm fully upward and hold the hand out away from your body, slightly to the right.
Sweep the flat hand in a smooth arc inward toward the center of your torso.
Finish the arc close to your chest, with the palm still facing upward.
Pair the gesture with a warm smile and an inviting posture toward the person.
Keep the movement generous and unhurried — it is a gesture of acceptance.
tip: “Welcomes” is signed with the base WELCOME sign.

steps: Open your dominant hand flat with the fingers together and extended.
Turn the palm fully upward and hold the hand out away from your body, slightly to the right.
Sweep the flat hand in a smooth arc inward toward the center of your torso.
Finish the arc close to your chest, with the palm still facing upward.
Pair the gesture with a warm smile and an inviting posture toward the person.
Keep the movement generous and unhurried — it is a gesture of acceptance.
tip: “Welcoming” is signed with the base WELCOME sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Open your dominant hand flat with the fingers together and extended.

Pair the gesture with a warm smile and an inviting posture toward the person.

tip: Past form of “Welcome” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Form a loose "C" handshape with each hand, fingertips curved and palms facing each other.
Raise both hands to the sides of your head, level with your temples.
Bring both hands down and inward toward your forehead in one smooth motion.
Finish with the C-hands resting at your temples, as if a wide-brimmed hat just settled onto your head.
tip: Plural of “President” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and open in front of your chest, palm facing up.
Raise your dominant index finger near your cheek, fingertip pointed toward the open palm.
Flick the index finger quickly toward the palm and tap it once, as if spotting something.
Aim the flick in the direction of the person or thing you noticed, since the sign is directional.
Keep a bright, alert expression to match the suddenness of noticing something.
tip: “Noticing” is signed with the base NOTICE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and open in front of your chest, palm facing up.
Raise your dominant index finger near your cheek, fingertip pointed toward the open palm.
Flick the index finger quickly toward the palm and tap it once, as if spotting something.
Aim the flick in the direction of the person or thing you noticed, since the sign is directional.
Keep a bright, alert expression to match the suddenness of noticing something.
tip: Past form of “Notice” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your chest with the palm facing up.
Bring the side of your dominant index finger down onto the center of that palm.
Repeat the downward tap at least once more with a quick, brisk motion.
Keep your face engaged and slightly animated, matching a lively back-and-forth conversation.
tip: Plural of “Discussion” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Touch your forehead with the tip of your dominant index finger, palm facing left.
Bring both index fingers together side by side in the space in front of your chest.
Press the fingertips together briefly with palms facing each other and hold the contact.
Give a small firm nod of the head as you finish, to show mutual understanding.
tip: Plural of “Agreement” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Raise your dominant hand to chest height in front of your torso.
Sweep the hand backward in a smooth arc that passes over your dominant shoulder.
Let the hand travel well behind the shoulder so the backward motion clearly reads as the past.
Keep your palm facing your body for the entire movement.
Make the arc larger and more emphatic when you mean long ago — a bigger sweep means further back.
tip: Plural of “Past” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an S handshape with your non-dominant hand, fingers curled tight with the thumb wrapped over them.
Turn that S hand palm-down and hold it steady in front of you.
Form an I handshape with your dominant hand, raising the pinkie upward.
Rest the dominant I hand on the back of the palm-down S hand.
Move the I hand in two horizontal circles — clockwise or counter-clockwise, either is fine.
tip: Plural of “Island” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand beside your head in a bent-hand shape, fingers together and curved.
Start with the hand near the side of your head, roughly at ear or temple height.
Shoot the hand upward quickly, letting it drift slightly forward as it rises.
Keep the movement short and brisk — it shows a person growing taller.
End with the hand clearly above its starting height, fingers still bent.
Stay neutral-faced; this sign also means TALL, so context picks the meaning.
tip: Plural of “Adult” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold up your non-dominant hand in a five handshape, palm facing toward your dominant side and fingers pointing up.
Flatten your dominant hand into a B shape, fingers together and thumb tucked in.
Slide the pinkie-side edge of the flat hand down between the middle and ring fingers of the raised hand.
Move it as if slipping a document into a file folder.
Do the insertion once for the verb 'to file', twice for the noun 'a file or document'.
Keep the raised hand steady and upright while the flat hand does the work.
tip: Plural of “Document” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of your torso as flat hands, palms facing down.
Keep your fingers together and the hands roughly shoulder-width apart.
Move both hands straight downward a few inches in one smooth, even motion.
Keep the hands level with each other through the whole drop.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression, since this is a plain noun sign.
tip: Plural of “Individual” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into S fists, with your thumbs folded across your fingers.
Hold the fists in front of your chest with the thumb sides facing each other and the palms facing down.
Strike the knuckle sides of your fists together.
Hit them together a second time, as if knocking two stones against each other.
Keep the strikes crisp and close to your chest, letting the soundless knock carry the meaning.
tip: Plural of “Rock” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend both index fingers upright, keeping your other fingers and thumbs tucked closed.
Hold the hands out in front of your chest about a foot apart, with your palms facing each other.
Bring the two hands toward each other until their lower edges meet in the middle.
Do not let the fingertips touch — the meeting happens at the base of the hands.
Aim the movement between the two people or spots to show who is meeting whom.
Keep your eyes on the meeting point and give a slight nod for a friendly greeting.
tip: “Meets” is signed with the base MEET sign.

steps: Form your dominant hand into an open X, with your thumb extended upward off the fist.
Raise the hand to about chin or forehead height in front of your body.
Pull the hand straight downward in one smooth motion toward your chest.
As the hand drops, fold the thumb down so it lands against your index finger's middle knuckle.
Finish with a closed X handshape, the thumb's knuckle tucked against the index finger.
Use a single downward pull for the verb; a double pull makes the noun SUBSCRIPTION.
tip: “Subscribes” is signed with the base SUBSCRIBE sign.

steps: Open your dominant hand into a five handshape with all fingers spread wide.
Bend only the middle finger forward at its large knuckle, leaving the other fingers straight and open.
Place the fingertip of the bent middle finger against your chest, directly over your heart.
Poke your chest twice with that fingertip in a quick, light double tap.
Hold the rest of the hand open and relaxed while the middle finger does the tapping.
Stay neutral-faced; the double poke at the heart carries the meaning of the sign.
tip: Plural of “Heart” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an H handshape with each hand, extending the index and middle fingers together.
Hold your non-dominant H hand flat and steady in front of your chest.
Set the dominant H hand on top of the non-dominant hand.
Rock the dominant hand back and forth in a quick double movement, like a balancing scale.
Keep the non-dominant hand completely still while the dominant hand does the rocking.
Stay neutral-faced; the rocking scale motion carries the meaning.
tip: Plural of “Weight” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands flat with the fingers held together in front of your chest.
Touch the fingertips of both hands together, forming the peaked shape of a rooftop.
Move both hands a little to the side while separating them slightly.
Touch the fingertips together again in the new position, forming a second rooftop.
Keep your palms angled down and toward each other so each rooftop keeps its peak.
Stay neutral-faced; the pair of rooftops stands for a town's buildings.
tip: Plural of “Town” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Bend both hands at the knuckles, keeping the fingers curved and relaxed.
Hold your non-dominant bent hand low in front of you as the base.
Lay your dominant bent hand directly on top of the base hand.
Alternate the hands, stacking each new layer on top of the last one.
Move the stack upward with every layer, as if building a wall higher.
Keep a neutral face; the upward stacking shows construction in progress.
tip: Plural of “Construction” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, curving your thumb and fingertips toward each other.
Hold the C-hand in front of your torso at the midline, beside your non-dominant hand, which stays still as a marker.
Slide the dominant hand sideways toward your dominant side in a short, firm path, like marking off a section.
Let the C-handshape open and flatten as it travels, finishing as a flat hand, palm facing down.
Keep your face neutral and relaxed — this is a straightforward content sign with no special grammar marker.
tip: Plural of “Chapter” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form both hands into hooked index-finger handshapes and stack them, with your dominant hand resting on top of the other.
Start the stacked hands off to one side of your signing space, near the person doing the lending.
Move the stacked hands in one straight path toward the borrower, as if passing an invisible object.
Keep the palms of the stacked hands facing down as they travel the full path.
Finish with the hands near the borrower — point the movement toward whoever receives the money or object.
tip: Plural of “Loan” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into fists, as if gripping a pair of horse reins.
Hold the fists in front of your chest about a foot apart, at the same height, palms facing inward.
Slide the hands alternately forward and back, like pulling reins to steer a horse.
Then add the agent marker: bring both flat hands to your sides with palms facing each other.
Glide the flat hands straight down past your torso to mean 'person,' completing the compound sign.
tip: Plural of “Manager” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of your torso as flat hands, palms facing down, as if each hand were a foot.
Keep your non-dominant hand still and low in front of you, acting as the back foot.
Lift your dominant hand up a few inches, letting the fingers tilt upward like a foot lifting off the ground.
Swing the raised hand forward past the stationary hand, moving in a short stepping arc.
Set the dominant hand down in its new forward position, finishing with both hands flat and palms down.
tip: “Stepping” is signed with the base STEP sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, with the thumb and fingers curved toward each other.
Close your non-dominant hand into a fist, with the thumb resting along the front of the fingers.
Rest the thumb of your C hand on the back of the fist, just behind the knuckles.
Tap the thumb up and down against the back of the fist, once or twice, in a straight vertical motion.
Keep the movement up and down only — never circle the thumb around.
Hold the fist steady in front of your chest and keep your face calm and neutral while signing.
tip: Plural of “Church” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make an A handshape with your dominant hand — a fist with the thumb resting up along the side.
Extend the index finger of your non-dominant hand and hold it out in front of you.
Brush the side of your dominant fist upward against the top edge of that index finger.
Repeat the brushing motion once or twice, keeping it small and controlled.
Keep the non-dominant index finger planted and steady while the fist brushes past it.
tip: “Practicing” is signed with the base PRACTICE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your chest in loose, relaxed 5-handshapes with your fingers slightly bent.
Angle both hands forward and slightly downward, with the fingertips pointing out and down.
Pump both hands forward and down, then back up, in a small repeated bouncing motion.
Keep your palms angled forward and down for the whole movement.
Use a relaxed, casual mouth shape, since chatting is informal, easy conversation.
tip: “Chats” is signed with the base CHAT sign.

steps: Extend both index fingers and hold your hands out in front of your torso, fingers pointing straight forward.
Curl the other fingers down into your palms and angle your palms slightly downward.
Flick both index fingers upward in one quick, sharp snapping motion.
Keep the movement brisk and short, ending with the fingertips pointing up.
tip: Plural of “Speed” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open your dominant hand into a 5-handshape with all fingers spread.
Hold the hand beside your face at cheek height, palm facing back toward your own face.
Draw one full circle around your face in the air, keeping the hand open the whole time.
Keep the palm facing back toward you as it circles.
tip: Plural of “Face” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Form both hands into H-handshapes, index and middle fingers extended together and pointing sideways.
Hold both hands close together in the signing space in front of your chest.
Turn your non-dominant palm down and your dominant palm up to start.
Move the dominant hand up and then down onto the non-dominant fingers, ending with the dominant palm facing down.
tip: “Increases” is signed with the base INCREASE sign.

steps: Form a Y-handshape with your dominant hand by stretching your thumb and pinkie wide while folding the middle fingers down.
Raise the hand to chest height in front of you with the palm facing down.
Press the hand firmly downward in one short, decisive stroke, as if pinning something in place.
Hold the Y-handshape rigid the whole time, keeping the thumb and pinkie fully extended.
Repeat the downward press with both hands together when you want extra emphasis.
Keep a firm, settled expression — this is a command to hold position, not a question.
tip: “Stays” is signed with the base STAY sign.

steps: Form a K-handshape with your dominant hand: point your index and middle fingers upward with the thumb tucked between them.
Set the K-hand just below your non-dominant shoulder at the top of your chest.
Sweep the hand diagonally across your torso in one straight stroke, ending near your opposite hip.
Keep the palm angled inward toward your body for the entire sweep.
Move smoothly and evenly — imagine tracing the sash a monarch wears across the chest.
Hold a neutral, dignified expression; a slight chin lift suits the royal meaning.
tip: Plural of “King” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of your torso at waist height with your palms facing down.
Keep your fingers relaxed and loosely open; do not curl or flex them at any point.
Churn both hands in an alternating circular motion, as if kneading a lump of dough.
Drive the movement from your shoulders and elbows, never from your wrists or fingers.
Continue the churning for a second or two with a steady, easy rhythm.
Keep a neutral, matter-of-fact expression — this is the general sign for being busy doing things.
tip: Plural of “Activity” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up, like a blank sheet of paper.
Reach your dominant open hand out over the flat hand with all five fingers spread.
Pinch the fingertips and thumb of the dominant hand together, as if lifting an invisible print off the page.
Pull the pinched hand back toward yourself in one smooth, short motion.
Set the pinched fingertips down onto the flat palm of your non-dominant hand.
Keep your expression neutral; the pinch-and-lift motion is what makes the sign readable.
tip: “Copies” is signed with the base COPY sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, fingers together, like a tray.
Position it at chest height so the flat palm is a clear landing surface.
Shape your dominant hand into a C above the far edge of that palm.
Pull the C hand back toward yourself along the length of the flat palm.
Close the C into a loose S fist while it travels, as if grabbing coins.
Keep the base hand's palm facing up and your face neutral throughout.
tip: Plural of “Income” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a G, thumb pinched against the bent index finger.
Hold the G hand beside your temple, a few inches out from your head.
Draw one small circle in the air next to your temple.
Finish by touching the fingertips lightly against your temple.
Angle the G so the fingertips point toward your head with a calm, neutral face.
tip: Plural of “Administration” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl both index fingers into hooked X shapes, as if each hand is pinching a tiny slip of paper.
Hold both hooked hands in front of your chest, about a foot apart.
Circle the two hands around each other once, trading places in the air.
End with both hands back where they started, the X hooks facing each other.
Keep a neutral face — the circling shows a straight swap with no tricks.
tip: “Exchanging” is signed with the base EXCHANGE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Press your thumbs together with the other fingers tucked into loose fists.
Hold the joined hands a few inches in front of your chest or upper belly.
Push both hands smoothly forward about six inches, away from your body.
Keep both palms angled downward for the whole forward glide.
Hold a steady, determined face — the motion says the action keeps going.
tip: “Continues” is signed with the base CONTINUE sign.
